nameStory: Black knot gets its straightforward name from the distinctive black, knobby growths it creates on tree branches. These rough, dark swellings look exactly like someone tied twisted black knots around the woody stems, making this one of the easiest plant diseases to name and remember.
description: Black knot is a fungal disease that attacks cherry, plum, and other stone fruit trees throughout New England. It creates distinctive rough, black growths that wrap around branches and twigs like ugly bracelets. These knots start small but can grow anywhere from 1 inch to 1 foot across, eventually strangling and killing the affected branches. While it was once a major threat to orchards, it's now mostly seen on wild trees and in poorly maintained fruit trees.

idTips.label: Black warty knots
idTips.description: Look for rough, coal-black swellings that completely encircle branches - they feel hard and crusty like burnt bark, with a distinctly warty, bumpy texture that's nothing like smooth tree bark

idTips.label: Olive-green early stage
idTips.description: In late spring, young infections appear as smooth, olive-green swellings that feel slightly soft and spongy to the touch before hardening into black knots

idTips.label: Branch girdling pattern
idTips.description: The growths wrap completely around twigs and branches like tight bands, causing the wood beyond the knot to die back and become brittle

idTips.label: Stone fruit tree hosts
idTips.description: Only found on cherry, plum, apricot, and chokecherry trees - never on apples, oaks, or other tree families

idTips.label: Woody parts only
idTips.description: Always grows on branches, twigs, or trunks - never on leaves, flowers, or fruit, and the wood around knots often cracks and splits

idTips.label: Insect activity
idTips.description: Older knots often have small holes and sawdust around them from beetles and other insects that tunnel into the diseased wood

habitat: Look for black knot anywhere stone fruit trees grow in New England - from abandoned farmsteads and old orchards to woodland edges where wild cherries and chokecherries thrive. It's especially common along roadsides, fence rows, and forest margins where wild Prunus species have established themselves. Urban and suburban areas with ornamental cherry or plum trees also harbor this disease.

seasonality.spring: New infections appear as small, olive-green swellings on branches that feel soft and slightly spongy. This is the best time to spot early-stage disease before it hardens.
seasonality.summer: Green swellings continue to expand and begin darkening around the edges. The growths feel firmer and start developing their characteristic rough texture.
seasonality.fall: Knots reach full development, turning completely black with their distinctive warty, crusty surface. This is when they're most obvious and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.winter: Black knots are highly visible against bare branches and snow. The dead wood beyond knots becomes brittle and may break off, leaving obvious stub ends.

funFact: Black knot essentially turns trees into insect apartment buildings - the diseased, weakened wood becomes a perfect home for beetles, borers, and other bugs that normally couldn't penetrate healthy bark, creating bustling communities of tiny tenants in what was once a thriving branch.
confusionNotes: Black knot might be mistaken for burls (woody growths), but burls are smooth and rounded while black knots are crusty and always girdle the entire branch. Remember: if it looks like a rough black bracelet choking a branch, it's black knot - if it's a smooth bulge growing from one side, it's probably a burl.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its dramatic appearance, black knot was historically one of the most devastating orchard diseases in North America during the 1800s, essentially forcing fruit growers to develop the pruning and spray programs still used today. Many cities now have black knot ordinances requiring property owners to remove infected trees to protect commercial orchards.
compareHints: Black knot is the only Apiosporina species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. It differs from other tree fungi by its exclusive preference for stone fruit trees and its distinctive girdling growth pattern that completely wraps around branches, unlike most other tree diseases that create patches, spots, or one-sided growths.
